title: Effects and Feasibility of the Transdiagnostic Dissociation Module (TDM): A Randomized Multiple-Baseline Pilot Study
summary:
Background: Dissociation describes experiences in which people feel disconnected from themselves, their feelings, their body, their memories, or the world around them. For example, they may feel as if they are outside their own body, as if they or the world around them are not real, or as if they are numb. Dissociation can occur in people with many different mental health problems and can be very distressing. Although dissociation is common, we still know little about how to best help people who experience severe dissociation. Dissociation can also make it harder to concentrate and learn new things. This may make it more difficult for people to benefit from psychotherapy.

Aim of the study: This pilot study will examine whether a short treatment program of eight sessions can help reduce severe dissociation. The Transdiagnostic Dissociation Module is designed for people who experience severe dissociation, regardless of what other mental health problems they may have. During treatment, participants learn to notice early signs of dissociation and use practical strategies to reduce or stop it. The treatment also focuses on factors that may make dissociation more likely, such as poor sleep, eating habits, and difficulties dealing with strong emotions. Some of these strategies have already been used in psychotherapy for people with posttraumatic stress disorder, where they have shown promising results in reducing dissociation.

Methods: People who experience severe dissociation will take part in the study. Before starting treatment, participants will wait for 3, 6, or 9 weeks. The length of the waiting period will be decided at random. After the waiting period, all participants will receive eight 50-minute therapy sessions over 8 to 12 weeks. Participants will regularly answer questions about their dissociation before, during, and after treatment. This will help us find out whether dissociation decreases more after treatment starts than during the waiting period. The main outcome of the study will be the severity of dissociation, measured using a standard questionnaire.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- A total score of at least 22 on the Dissociation-Tension Scale (DSS; Stiglmayr et al., 2010), to ensure a sufficient level of dissociative experiences
- Presence of a mental disorder
- Sufficient proficiency in German
- Sufficient ability to communicate with the study staff and to complete the questionnaires
Exclusion criteria:
- Current suicidal intent requiring inpatient treatment, or a suicide attempt within the past 2 months
- Acute psychotic disorder
- Current manic episode in the context of bipolar I disorder
- Current severe alcohol or substance use disorder without at least 2 months of abstinence (except nicotine and caffeine)
- Ongoing outpatient, day-patient, or inpatient psychotherapy, or psychotherapy planned during the study period
- Initiation or change of psychopharmacological treatment within the past 4 weeks
- Current benzodiazepine medication
- Planned absence of more than 4 weeks during the 6 months following study enrollment
